list.listitem: Symptoms of dysuria plus a positive dipstick test result for nitrites is best to rule in UTI. A
Healthy women complaining of dysuria may be phone triaged and empirically treated for a UTI. C

Women reporting vaginal discharge/odor or at risk for a sexually transmitted disease (STD) should undergo a pelvic examination with samples obtained for KOH, wet prep, and a gonococcal (GC)/chlamydia probe. C
Dysuria alone in men suggests a chlamydial urethritis. Tenderness and bogginess of the prostate suggest prostatitis, whereas tenderness of the testes suggests acute epididymo-orchitis. C
Several well validated clinical prediction rules exist to aid in the diagnosis of UTI in adults and children with dysuria (see below). C
Genital vesicles or tiny ulcerations in female or male patients is suspicious for herpes simplex virus (HSV): nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) or viral culture may be used for confirmation. C
PCR is preferred if available over wet mount microscopy to diagnosis trichomonas vaginalis. C

background.definition: Dysuria is defined as pain, tingling, or burning during or just after urination.

list.listitem: Approximately 25% of adult women will experience an episode of dysuria each year.
Six in 1000 women per year will seek medical attention for significant UTI symptoms; only 1 per 1000 men will seek care.
In men, dysuria becomes more common with increasing age.
Dysuria accounts for up to 5% of visits to family physicians.

For suspected UTI, immediate use of antibiotics or using a dipstick test to evaluate for nitrites, leukocyte esterase or blood is more cost effective than sending mid-stream urine for culture, delayed antibiotics, or using a symptom score.
UTIs caused by Escherichia coli (up to 85% of the time) or other "uropathogens," for example, Staphylococcus saprophyticus (mostly in young women), Klebsiella sp., Proteus mirabilis, and enterococci.
STDs: chlamydia, gonorrhea, trichomonas, herpes virus.
Candidal vaginitis in women.
Urethritis, prostatitis, or epididymitis in men.
Pain receptors are triggered when urine is passed through tissues of the bladder or urethra that are inflamed as a result of infection.
Inflammation of labial tissue also triggers pain receptors when the urine stream hits the labia.

Differential.Differential_Features: Midstream sample for urinalysis and/or culture
Microscopic examination of discharge: KOH and wet mount
Examine tissues for ulcerations and culture if needed
Microscopic examination (Gram stain) of discharge or urinalysis of first voided specimen
Examine vaginal tissues for drying and thinning mucosa; topical estrogen relieves symptoms
History demonstrates temporal relation between substance and symptom
Urine specimen (wait 2 hours to void) for nucleic acid amplification test
Cervical probe (30 seconds in os) or urine specimen (wait 2 hours to void)

list.listitem: Self-diagnosis of UTI in women (LR+ 4.0) is a good predictor of having a laboratory confirmed UTI. Absence of vaginal discharge (LR+ 3.1) or irritation (LR+ 2.7) are also good predictors of UTI.
Women 18 to 49 years: The best predictors of UTI in women with suspected UTI include hematuria (LR+ 3.0), nocturia (LR+ 1.8) and dysuria (LR+ 1.6).
Women 50 years and older: The best predictors of UTI include offensive urine odor (LR+ 2.1), nocturia (LR+ 1.8), and dysuria (LR+ 1.6).
In men with suspected UTI, hematuria (LR+ 29) and offensive urine odor (LR+ 28) are strong predictors of UTI.

Symptoms that best predict UTI in men are hematuria, nausea, dysuria, and self-diagnosis. They may also complain of itching or discharge at the meatus, urgency, frequency, or nocturia. The examination should include inspection and palpation of the entire pubic area, including lymph nodes, penis, and testicles. Dysuria alone in men suggests chlamydial infection.
Tenderness and bogginess of the prostate suggest prostatitis, whereas tenderness of the testes suggests acute epididymo-orchitis.
Dysuria is not associated with testicular torsion, but may be associated with candidal vaginitis.
In children, urinary frequency (LR+ 41) as well as offensive urine odor (LR+ 3.0), urgency (LR+ 2.6), and nocturia (LR+ 2.2) predict UTI in children.
Sexual history should include last menstrual period, type of contraception, recent sexual activity, and history of STDs.
Women reporting vaginal discharge/odor or at risk for an STD should undergo a pelvic examination with samples obtained for KOH, wet prep, and GC/chlamydia probe.

In sexually active women without vaginal symptoms, acute cystitis is the most likely diagnosis when chief complaint is dysuria. Pyelonephritis should be suspected with costovertebral angle tenderness and fever.
Consider a UTI in men with any of the following risk factors: recent intercourse with a female partner with a UTI, homosexuality, or noncircumcised.
Genital vesicles or tiny ulcerations in female or male patients suggest HSV; nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) or viral culture may be used for confirmation.
Clean-catch urine samples do not decrease specimen contamination.
Culture specimens considered positive for UTI on a variety of colony counts (102, 103, 105 CFU/ml), most consider 105 CFU/ml to be the gold standard.
Three dipstick findings independently predict UTI: nitrite, leukocyte esterase, and blood.

Urinary flow cytometry (UFC) can accurately identify leukocytes and bacteria and rule out urinary tract infection if negative. A systematic review of the accuracy of UFC found that when using microbiologically defined bacteriuria thresholds of 105, 104 and 103 CFU/ml, the negative predictive values were 98%, 91%, and 89% and positive predictive values were 67%, 72% and 73% using a cut-off of 250 bacteria/μl.
For men with dysuria, urethral microscopy is positive in 67% with a discharge, but also in 33% without a discharge.

Direct microscopy and culture may fail to detect trichomonas in men, with a study finding that 6.5% of men referred to a urology clinic were positive by PCR for T. vaginalis but none were seen using microscopy or culture. A Ugandan study found the same thing in women with a sensitivity of 25% for wet mount microscopy and 92% for PCR to detect T. vaginalis.

A study involving 4181 consecutive children <36 months of age undergoing bladder catheterization for clinically suspected UTI reported that the accuracy of dipstick leukocyte esterase 1+ or higher in all children was 81% sensitive and 95% specific (LR+ 16, LR- 0.19), and in those with fever was 84% sensitive and 95% specific (LR+ 16.8, LR- 0.17). Having 5 or more WBC per HPF on microscopy was 78% sensitive and 88% specific (LR+ 6.5, LR- 0.25), while in those with fever it was 86% sensitive and 89% specific (LR+ 7.8, LR- 0.16). Given the absence of pyuria in about 20% of these febrile children diagnosed with UTI (by culture), the authors question the soundness of requiring pyuria to diagnose UTI in this age group.
A machine learning model has been developed and externally validated in a primary care setting to predict positive urine culture.

See chapters on urinary tract infection in adults, urinary tract infection in children, HSV, urethritis (male), urethritis (female), chlamydia, and gonorrhea for more information on diagnostic tests for those conditions.
A simple 5 item clinical score from Wigton and colleagues has been validated to diagnose UTI in women.
A second simple 5 item clinical prediction rule from Leibovici and colleagues has been validated to diagnose UTI in women age 20 to 39 years.
McIsaac and colleagues validated a 4 item clinical prediction rule for diagnosing UTI in women.
The two-step DUTY score can diagnose UTI in children age 5 and younger.
Symptoms such as dysuria, frequency, hematuria, and back pain may help predict UTI, but dipstick findings of nitrite or leukocyte esterase increase the positive predictive value.
Patients who call complaining of dysuria may be triaged over the phone and treated for UTI with 3 days of trimethoprim/sulfa (or other appropriate antibiotic if sulfa allergic).
Managment of UTI with immediate antibiotics, a symptom based score, mid-stream urine culture, dipstick results, or delayed antibiotics all result in similar symptom control.
Antibiotic use after a dipstick test for nitrites, leukocytes, or blood may help reduce antibiotic use, which in turn may help reduce antibiotic resistance.
See algorithm in and for evaluation in female and male patients.
